G-F021.trick: Like dissolves like: small, oily (nonpolar) molecules slip right through the oily membrane.
G-F021.tip: O2 and CO2 cross by simple diffusion. Ions and big polar molecules need a protein channel or carrier.

G-F022.trick: TIGHT junction = a zip-lock seal. Desmosome = a rivet. GAP junction = a doorway.
G-F022.tip: Match the junction to the job: seal (tight), hold together under stress (desmosome), pass signals (gap).

G-F023.trick: LYSOsome = LYSE (break apart). It's the cell's recycling and garbage center.
G-F023.tip: Undigested debris building up points to lysosomes. Peroxisomes detoxify; mitochondria make ATP.

G-F024.trick: MICROvilli = a fuzzy bath towel: lots of little folds = lots of surface to soak things up.
G-F024.tip: Microvilli absorb (more surface), cilia sweep (motion), a flagellum swims. Don't mix up absorption and movement.

G-F025.trick: Diffusion hates distance: a thicker wall = a longer trip = slower rate.
G-F025.tip: Diffusion is faster with more area, a bigger concentration difference, and a thinner barrier.

G-F026.trick: HYPO-tonic = the cell swells like a HIPPO (water rushes in).
G-F026.tip: Water moves toward more solute. A cell that swells or bursts was in a hypotonic solution.

G-F027.trick: SECONDARY active = riding someone else's wave. Sodium rolls downhill and drags the other solute up.
G-F027.tip: If the carrier itself doesn't use ATP but moves something uphill using an ion gradient, it is secondary active transport.

G-F028.trick: EXOcytosis = EXIT the cell. ENDOcytosis = ENTER the cell.
G-F028.tip: Vesicle fusing with the membrane and dumping contents outside = exocytosis (how hormones and neurotransmitters leave).

G-F029.trick: PMAT order. TELOphase = TWO new nuclei form at the far ends (telo = end).
G-F029.tip: Prophase condenses, metaphase lines up, anaphase pulls apart, telophase rebuilds the nuclei.

G-F030.trick: Benign = stays put, but even a quiet tenant can crowd the house.
G-F030.tip: Benign means no invasion and no spread. It can still cause harm by pressing on nearby structures.

C-ch3-membrane.trick: The plasma membrane is a bouncer: it picks who gets in (selectively permeable).
C-ch3-membrane.tip: "Selectively permeable" is the key phrase for the plasma membrane. It is made of phospholipids and proteins.
C-ch3-membrane.why: The plasma membrane is the cell's selectively permeable boundary: a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. The nuclear envelope surrounds only the nucleus, the cytoskeleton is the cell's internal protein framework, and a basement membrane is the layer outside the cell that epithelium sits on.

C-ch3-organelles.trick: ORGAN-elle = a tiny organ inside the cell.
C-ch3-organelles.tip: Each organelle has one main job. Know them: ribosome makes protein, mitochondria make ATP, Golgi packages.
C-ch3-organelles.why: An organelle is a specialized structure inside a cell with a particular job, such as a mitochondrion or the Golgi apparatus. The cytosol is the fluid around the organelles, inclusions are stored materials like glycogen granules, and an organ is a much larger structure made of several tissues.

C-ch3-nucleus.trick: CHROMATIN = loose spaghetti DNA; it coils into chromosomes only for division.
C-ch3-nucleus.tip: Chromatin = DNA + proteins, spread out between divisions. Chromosomes = condensed chromatin during mitosis.
C-ch3-nucleus.why: Chromatin is DNA wound around proteins, spread loosely through the nucleus between divisions; it condenses into chromosomes for mitosis. A chromatid is one copy of a duplicated chromosome, the nucleolus builds ribosome subunits, and nuclear pores control traffic through the envelope.

C-ch3-diffusion.trick: Diffusion = a drop of food coloring spreading in water: high to low, no energy needed.
C-ch3-diffusion.tip: Down the gradient = passive (no ATP). Against the gradient = active (needs energy).
C-ch3-diffusion.why: Diffusion is net movement of a substance from higher to lower concentration, driven by random molecular motion and needing no ATP. Osmosis is the special case of water crossing a membrane, filtration is driven by pressure, and active transport spends energy to move substances against a gradient.

C-ch3-osmosis.trick: Osmosis = water chasing solute (like salt) across a membrane.
C-ch3-osmosis.tip: Osmosis is only about WATER moving. If a solute moves, it is diffusion or transport instead.
C-ch3-osmosis.why: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with more effective (nonpenetrating) solute. Tonicity describes a solution's effect on cell volume, hypotonic describes a solution that makes cells swell, and filtration is driven by pressure.

C-ch3-active.trick: Active transport = pushing a cart uphill: it needs fuel (ATP).
C-ch3-active.tip: "Against the gradient" means active transport. The Na+/K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP.
C-ch3-active.why: Active transport uses energy, directly or indirectly from ATP, to move a substance against its electrochemical gradient, like the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Facilitated diffusion, osmosis and filtration are all passive: they move substances down a gradient without spending ATP.

C-ch3-cycle.trick: INTERphase = the cell's "in-between" prep time: Grow (G1), Synthesize DNA (S), Get ready (G2).
C-ch3-cycle.tip: DNA copies during the S phase of interphase, not during mitosis.
C-ch3-cycle.why: Interphase is the part of the cell cycle between divisions: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (getting ready). Mitosis divides the nucleus, starting with prophase, and cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm.

C-ch3-differentiation.trick: Stem cell = a blank tree trunk that can grow any branch AND keep the trunk.
C-ch3-differentiation.tip: Two features define a stem cell: it renews itself and it can make specialized cells.
C-ch3-differentiation.why: A stem cell can both renew itself (make more stem cells) and give rise to specialized, differentiated cells. A differentiated cell has already specialized, a malignant cell divides out of control and can invade, and a gamete is an egg or sperm.
